paper_title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models have reduced the effort required to generate code for software [22], increasing the importance of effective verification [37]. In interactive software, testing target behavior may require long sequence of prerequisite interactions [46], repeated across commits. Automated tests for such software often start from hand-built fixtures, leaving states beyond them hard to verify [19, 26, 49]. The shortfall is sharpest in games, where developers report substantially less test automation than in other domains [33] and only 7.33% of 491 open-source projects contain automated tests [7]. The cost of covering these states depends on how much of the running application test harness can read and write, and the self-rendered engines widely used in game development expose little of it (Appendix A.1). Unit tests alone are insuﬀicient: GUI-specific failures (e.g., softlock, where the software keeps running but the player cannot progress [8]) may emerge only during full interaction sequence [37], and industrial reports rank progress-blocking failures among the most common defects [42]. GUI automation based on reusable Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. Figure 1 GUI agent reaches the deep state through long pixel-action sequence, whereas StatePortal synthesizes checkpoint and restores the target state directly. The two pixel routes represent GUI agents, and their E2E rates and mean token costs are measured with Agent S3 [15] on gpt-5.6-terra over the 61 tasks. DOM selectors [50] does not transfer to self-rendered engines, which expose no element tree. pixel agent replaying an n-step path instead requires O(n) model decisions, whose errors can compound over the sequence [11] and whose inference cost recurs on every regression run. We study deep-state GUI testing: testing behavior that cannot be reached from the initial screen with small number of actions [46]. Prior works rely on platform-specific state-inspection mechanisms that do not carry over to self-rendered engines, or generate test code without constructing the state it requires (Section 6). From functional test case, we instead synthesize checkpoint, reusable artifact that restores target state (the Start) through callable state-transition interface (the hook) that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes from the applications source. Our agent StatePortal (Figure 1) explores the repository to identify the relevant state representation, persistence path, and transition logic. It jointly generates the Start, restoration payload, bounded transition spec, and predicted assertions as one executable checkpoint. Restoration inside running application (a warm session) replaces the n-step prefix. Whether the Start is restored or reached through pixel actions, every trial is checked against the same hidden targets on runtime state and screenshots. Existing GUI-agent benchmarks do not evaluate checkpoint synthesis for new target from test case and read-only source  (Table 1)  . We therefore build DeepStateBench: 61 tasks over ten applications (seven games and three general-purpose GUI applications), each scored by conjunctive oracle under which programmatic-state oracle and visual oracle must both pass, since state checks alone can miss failures visible only in rendered output [25, 45]. The suite spans five language families and six rendering stacks, all restored through one shared hook contract. Across three registered decision models, checkpoint seeding increases GUI-agent completion from 0% to 10.4% under the same pixel action space. StatePortal, which also executes the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Checkpoints support regression testing without further synthesis (98.90% verdict reproduction over 1,361 replays), the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% of controlled visual faults that leave registered state fields unchanged. On real defects that the repositorys own tests miss, StatePortals checkpoints separate buggy from fixed builds on 7 of 8 comparable tasks. In summary, we make the following four contributions: task formulation: from functional test case and read-only source, synthesize checkpoint that restores the Start and runs the transition under test (Section 2). StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes the Start and the transition jointly from one source exploration, with hooks onboarded for all ten applications without human intervention (Section 3). 2 conjunctive evaluation protocol in which programmatic-state oracle and VLM judge must both pass, so the judge can overturn programmatic pass but never failure (Section 4.3). DeepStateBench, 61 public tasks over ten applications of up to 7.2M lines. Unlike other GUI-agent benchmarks, it provides the source and leaves the Start to the method (Section 4).

sections.title: 2 Task Definition
sections.content: We study checkpoint synthesis for functional testing of stateful applications. method receives pair (u, R): natural-language functional test case derived from bug report or feature request and read-only access to the targets source repository R. For each test, the method needs to output single configuration file, the checkpoint, declaring the semantic state to restore (the Start), the strategy and payload that construct it, finite transition spec (the post-Start action sequence under test), and assertions over the resulting state. The declared Start is constructed through per-application hook, callable state-transition interface that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes from source once per application. The same agent writes the hooks capability contract Σ = h(R, B), declarative file specifying the hook kind, its activation gate, its calling convention, and the readable and writable state fields, with the public onboarding brief of Section 3.4. Σ contains neither per-test state assignments nor hidden grading criteria. checkpoint is synthesized as ˆc = g(u, G, Σ), where denotes the source evidence retrieved during exploration of the sandboxed repository R. Validity is checked in two gated stages. ValidStart requires that the restored state match the declared Start, the runtime stay healthy, the frame be ready, and, for save-restorable checkpoint, the persisted state roundtrip through save/reload cycle. After Start validity and the hidden Start oracles pass, ValidTrans checks that the transition spec executes without error. Section 4.3 scores whether the restored and post-transition states match the graders respective hidden Start and post-transition criteria. The graders reference specifications and oracle remain hidden throughout synthesis: states the scenario as human tester would without exposing the graders internal reference specification, and leakage guard rejects trials that access oraclereserved paths (Algorithm 1, Table 6).

sections.title: 3 Method: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis
sections.content: StatePortal translates functional test case into an executable checkpoint through source-grounded exploration, semantic checkpoint construction, and joint transition synthesis. Given u, bounded map of R, and the onboarding contract Σ (Section 3.4), one model emits the checkpoint and its transition in single final response from one shared exploration history (Figure 2).

sections.content: The agent identifies the objects, identifiers, and control flow relevant to the task scenario through bounded ReAct loop [47] over list_dir, grep, and read_file. sections.content: Before task construction, source-guided onboarding agent reads the clean upstream repository and, from capability brief and runtime notes, generates the hook, driver, Σ, and save/reload self-tests, validated on five cases per application (two held out). Each synthesis trial then evaluates single candidate without runtime or hidden-oracle feedback, with at most one repair of its output structure from public feedback. sections.title: 4 Benchmark Suite and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Evaluating the method requires software with accessible source code, target states that require long interaction sequences, and evaluation oracles hidden from the agent. The eleven benchmarks in Table 1 do not jointly satisfy these requirements. We therefore introduce DeepStateBench: 10 applications and 61 public tasks derived mechanically from source evidence. In DeepStateBench, constructing the Start is part of the task: the synthesized checkpoint must restore valid state in the running software and support the target action. Six applications render to single GPU surface without DOM or accessibility tree. Evaluation therefore combines programmatic runtime-state checks with screenshot-based checks, and trial passes only when both do.

sections.title: 4.1 Benchmark Composition
sections.content: The suite spans two Unity RPGs, three browser games, Luanti, OpenRA, JupyterLab, LibreOﬀice, and Blender (Figures 3 and 4, Table 5). These applications comprise 10.9M lines of source across five language families and six rendering stacks, ranging from 874 lines for 2048 to 2.8M for Blender and 7.2M for LibreOﬀice. All share the hook contract, checkpoint schema, and evaluation protocol. Seven application profiles (46 tasks) are games, including four self-rendered games that form our primary target domain, and the remaining three (15 tasks) are general-purpose applications. Table 5 also records the channel through which each tasks registered transition spec delivers the target action. The channel is property of the task: Agent S3 and Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint always act through pixels, and every trial is scored against the same hidden targets.

sections.title: 4.2 Metric-Grounded Task Provenance
sections.content: Each task is produced by three-stage mechanical pipeline driven by fixed public inputs (Appendix B.5). Selection converts per-function complexity, nesting, fan-in/fan-out, and gitchurn signals [16, 30, 34] into percentile ranks combined under weights frozen before ranking, then keeps the regions whose state is observable and controllable through discovered semantic surface, as execution-based benchmarks in the OSWorld lineage [45] also require. The criterion admits only deterministic transitions expressible through that interface. Ground truth is recorded from one controlled real execution of branchcovering seed states through the hook. These seeds and their follow-on actions are the pipelines only authored input, and assertions are restricted to the replay-stable projection of the after-state. Discrimination confines language-agnostic singlepoint mutants [9, 18] to the regions line span and excludes regions with low mutation kill rates. final phrasing step paraphrases the specification into bug-report-style issue under guard requiring equivalence of the specification tokens. Four gates verify the pipeline  (Table 8)  : re-running selection reproduces the ranking, and on the 2048 pilot region, assertions hold on an unpinned run (3/3), the leakage guard passes on both phrasing variants (6/6), and the oracle kills 7 of 8 mutants. Catalog-wide, all 61 oracle-built references pass both programmatic qualification runs (122/122, Table 27). Figure 4 The 61 tasks by profile, colored by domain family (full form, Figure 5).

sections.title: 4.3 Hybrid Programmatic-State and Visual Evaluation
sections.content: A checkpoint may satisfy registered state checks while producing an incorrect rendered frame. We therefore evaluate both semantic state and visual output. trial runs in two phases, Phase establishing the Start and Phase executing the bounded target action in the live software. registered gate between them runs the programmatic Start check first, then the visual check on frame captured with the runtime suspended, and both channels are checked again for the Goal verdict. Acceptance is the conjunction Oprog Ovis of Programmatic State Oracle, which reads semantic state fields, persistence round-trips, and runtime health, and VLM Oracle, which grades each gates frame against that stages golden reference and rubric of what must, must not, and may appear. Visual rubrics tolerate benign non-determinism and leave value-level checks to the programmatic oracle. Conjunction imposes monotonicity constraint: Ovis can downgrade trial that passes the programmatic oracle to failure but cannot accept trial that fails it, so skipping visual evaluation when Oprog = Fail saves VLM call and leaves the verdict unchanged (Appendix B.11). Cross-VLM calibration. The evaluation judge is single fixed model, qwen3-vl-flash. Two blinded VLM annotators (glm-5.3-flash and doubao-seed-2-1-turbo) independently label every sample, and claude-sonnet-5 adjudicates only disagreements and uncertain labels. The 200 samples are independent of every study in Section 5: 40 base states drawn under frozen hash, each expanded into clean before-frame, clean after-frame, same-profile wrong state, blank render, and distributed striped occlusion. sections.title: 5.1.1 Checkpoint Synthesis: Cost and Accuracy
sections.content: The performance study examines two factors: the source of the Start state and the interface used to execute the target action. Agent S3 [15] runs from the initial screen with pixel execution. Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint restores StatePortal-synthesized Start, then executes only the target action with the same policy and pixel action space, isolating state construction. StatePortal restores the same kind of Start but delivers the target action as the transition spec from the exploration that produced the checkpoint, isolating the execution interface. All three run on all 61 tasks under three decision models (gpt-5.6-terra, gemini-3.5-flash, and kimi-k2.6) and seeds 02: 1,647 registered trials in Latin-square rotation blocked by model and seed, 549 per configuration. Table 2 adds second pixel-policy family, CUA Agent and CUA Agent w/ Checkpoint, which run ScaleCUA [28] cold and seeded, and fourth decision model, gpt-6-astra [35]. These extension rows (n = 183 each) are never pooled with the registered aggregates. State construction under fixed pixel policy. Pooled across models and seeds, Agent S3 reaches Start on 7.8% of trials and 0% E2E success, using 408.3k tokens on average, whereas Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint reaches Start on 36.6% and records 10.4% E2E (task-clustered bootstrap 95% CI [4.9, 16.6]) at 163.8k mean tokens. Per-model exact McNemar tests are significant after Holm correction (p 0.00195). At the request level 7 (Figure 6), checkpoint seeding cuts the 42.4 requests per completed trial of Agent S3 to 16.2, and StatePortal to 7.4. restore takes only 13 s. Execution interface after checkpoint restoration. StatePortal reaches Start on 38.4% of trials and records 27.5% E2E (95% CI [19.3, 36.1]) at 106.7k mean tokens. Because comparison with Agent S3 changes both factors, the informative contrast is Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint, which restores Start from the same synthesis agent at similar rate (36.6%). The 17.1-point E2E gap between the two supports the benefit of delivering the target action through the generated transition spec. Joint synthesis versus delegated planning. In the diagnostic StatePortal-Delegated, separate bounded planner generates the target action from the test-case text, outside the exploration that built the Start. It records 24.2% E2E against 27.5%  (Table 22)  . It reaches Start more often (43.9% versus 38.4%) but converts fewer Starts into Goal successes (55.2% versus 71.6%, 16.4-point difference with CI [7.0, 25.9]), consistent with jointly synthesized transition fitting its checkpoint better. Additional pixel policies and decision models. On the matched population (Table 19, = 183 per configuration), cold CUA Agent reaches Start on 8.712.6% of trials and records at most 1.6% E2E, against 7.18.7% Start and no E2E success for Agent S3 under the three registered models. Seeded, CUA Agent w/ Checkpoint and Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint both record 5.514.2% E2E against 22.435.5% for StatePortal. The same ordering holds for gpt-6-astra, whose two cold configurations reach at most 3.8% E2E: at similar Start rates (46.4 48.1%), both seeded pixel configurations reach 14.2% E2E and StatePortal 30.6%, at 135.7k mean tokens against 248.9k for cold Agent S3.

sections.title: 5.1.2 Checkpoint Reuse: Reliability and Regression Cost
sections.content: The replay study re-executes frozen checkpoints through the execution and grading path of the performance study, with all model calls disabled. We replay 112 checkpoints from 8 profiles 513 times each across two environments, for 1,361 graded replays. Of these, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict (bootstrap 95% CI [96.8%, 100%], clustered by checkpoint), including all 328 replays of the 29 checkpoints accepted in the performance study. The median replay takes 422 ms. One checkpoint is inconsistent across replays, and one other is consistent but differs from its original verdict (Appendix B.24). Because replay adds no model calls, StatePortals cumulative token cost stays below both Agent S3 configurations from the first run on, for every model (gpt-5.6-terra, first run: 51.6k against 302.0k for cold Agent S3 and 96.6k for Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint). Answer to RQ1: StatePortal improves test completion and enables reuse without model calls. Most of the cost of deep-state testing lies in reaching the state rather than in the tested action, so checkpoint synthesized once amortizes that cost over model-free, sub-second replays.

sections.title: 5.2 RQ2: Can checkpoint synthesis expose real defects the registered tests miss?
sections.content: The latent-defect study asks whether synthesized checkpoints expose visual defects that the registered tests miss while the software keeps running [37]. Its population  (Table 23)  is 11 real issues with merged fixes (6 JupyterLab, 3 Luanti, 2 OpenRA) that have no fail-to-pass (F2P) test: every registered pass-to-pass (P2P) test passes on both the fixed version and the buggy version, which we reconstruct by reversing the fixs production-code changes. F2P absence is an admission requirement, because issue-to-test generation succeeds on about one third of real issues or fewer [3, 19, 32] and defects confined to rendered output require visual evaluation [29]. Both versions must reach visually equivalent Start states before their post-transition outputs are compared. Agent S3 and CUA Agent reach Start from the initial screen through pixel actions, whereas Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint, CUA Agent w/ Checkpoint, and StatePortal restore shared synthesized checkpoint, after which the first two act through pixels and StatePortal through generated semantic actions. The comparison covers four decision models, two versions, and five configurations: 440 cells, 88 each. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: GUI and computer-use agents. Pixel-driven GUI agents such as the Agent line [1, 2, 15], ScaleCUA [28], and UI-TARS [39] map screenshot observations to coordinate-based actions. OSWorld and OSWorld-2 established execution-grounded, programmatic-state scoring for computer-use evaluation [45, 48], and OS-Harm shows that such an oracle can miss failures observable only in rendered output [25]. Our hybrid oracle keeps the programmatic channel as the necessary condition and adds visual channel under an explicit monotonicity constraint. None of these evaluations asks the agent to synthesize the deep starting state itself. Benchmarks for GUI agents and game testing. Agent benchmarks score navigation or task completion in benchmark-prepared environments, on desktop and professional software [5, 12, 27, 45], on mobile, web, and multi-platform GUIs [14, 17, 24, 41, 44], on full story arcs in adventure games [4], and on exploratory defect discovery [13]  (Table 1)  . LLM agents play-test games, where progress-blocking failures rank among the most common defects [42] and softlocks are recognized level-design hazard [8]. PlayCoder checks whether LLM-generated GUI code is playable [37], and VisionDroid finds non-crash functional bugs from the screen [29]. State construction in software testing. Android GUI testing reaches deep states without full replay by constructing launching contexts [46], snapshotting and rolling back VM state [10], and recomposing mined use-case fragments [40, 43]. These approaches use Android-specific state-inspection mechanisms, whereas StatePortal generates hook and capability contract for each application (Section 3.4). Hand-written fixtures and debug save states [36, 38] provide reusable starting states but require developers to encode them. further line generates executable tests from natural language, by reproducing described bug [21, 32, 49] or by synthesizing end-to-end test scripts from specification [6, 20, 23]. Our task additionally requires valid application-native checkpoints.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes deep-state checkpoints from functional test case and readonly source, and DeepStateBench, 61 tasks over ten applications scored by conjunctive oracle. Our results support checkpoint synthesis as complementary mechanism for deep-state GUI testing. Under the same pixel action space and conjunctive oracle, seeding Agent S3 with synthesized checkpoints raises completion from 0% to 10.4%, and StatePortal, which also executes the transition through the hook, completes 27.5% (Section 5.1). Replays reproduce 98.90% of 1,361 verdicts without model calls, including every replay of an accepted checkpoint. On real repairs missed by every registered test, StatePortals checkpoints separate the buggy and fixed versions on 7 of 8 comparable tasks in this diagnostic study. Extending it to more real repairs and seeds would measure how reliably synthesized tests separate regressions from fixes. We open-source our code and benchmark at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to help polish portions of the manuscript text (including translation and language editing). We also used generative AI tools to help write data-conversion scripts. We did not use generative AI tools to design the research methodology, formulate the papers claims, or interpret the reported results. sections.title: Ethics statement
sections.content: This work involves no human-subjects data collection: the only annotation used anywhere in the paper is blinded, model-only cross-VLM labeling (Section 4.3), with no crowdworker or other human annotator data. All ten benchmark applications  (Table 5)  are open-source software exercised locally under their licenses; no production service or third-party user data is accessed.

sections.title: Reproducibility statement
sections.content: The experimental protocol (models, seeds, etc.) is specified in Section 5.1.1, with the manifest/content hashes, and per-stage gates in the appendix sections, and the benchmarks mechanical task-provenance pipeline (selection, ground truth, discrimination, and the four gates of Table 8) is detailed in Section 4.2 and Appendix B.5. The appendix further gives the checkpoint-synthesis algorithm (B.3), the hook-onboarding protocol and its independent replication (B.6), the pixel action space of the Agent S3 and CUA Agent baselines (B.15), the harness configuration keys (B.8), the runtime-hold and Start-parity protocols (B.13 and B.14), the delegated-transition diagnostic (B.19), the execution-channel strata and the CUA Agent failure audit (B.17 and B.18), the evaluation-eﬀiciency and reference-control analyses (B.23 and B.24), and the complete per-model, per-seed, and per-task result tables underlying every number in Section 5 (B.16 B.21). Every reported statistic is computed from archived run records by the result-aggregation and evidencecollection procedures, which verify task, specification, and report hashes before generating any table. The supplementary evidence includes aggregate results and complete trial-level records. sections.title: A Motivation
sections.content: A.1 Motivating Example The cost of deep-state testing is not uniform across interactive software: it depends almost entirely on what the runtime lets test harness reach into. We make this concrete by contrasting one end of the spectrum, browser game whose entire state is addressable from the test process, with the other end, engine-backed software, whose state the harness cannot reach. The cheap end: browser game. SpaceRPG ships Playwright suite in which single test walks the first two chapters of the main storyline: an opening cinematic, mission acceptance, an inter-system jump, docking, two boss kills, salvage recovery, and debriefing at second station. Listing 1 abridges that 140-line TypeScript test to its two load-bearing steps. Listing 1 Abridged SpaceRPG smoke test with story names neutralized. Comments are ours. test("smokes the first two story chapters", async ({ page }) => { await resetApp(page); await startNewGame(page, { keepIntro: true }); // (1) The store is callable from the test process through window handle, so the // dialogue can be dismissed by name rather than by locating and clicking control. await page.evaluate(() => { (window.__SPACERPG_E2E__!.getState() as { closeDialogue: () => void }).closeDialogue(); }); // ... accept the first mission, then jump systems and dock via the store's own actions ... // (2) Kill the first boss deterministically instead of aiming and firing in real time: // co-locate the player and the target at the origin, push every other enemy far away // so it cannot interfere, inject one lethal projectile owned by the player, and then // advance the simulation by exactly one fixed 50 ms step. await page.evaluate(() => { const e2e = window.__SPACERPG_E2E__!; const state = e2e.getState() as { player: Record<string, unknown>; runtime: { enemies: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; projectiles: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; } }; e2e.setState({ targetId: "scout-drone", player: { ...state.player, position: [0, 0, 0] }, runtime: { ...state.runtime, enemies: state.runtime.enemies.map((ship) => ship.id === "scout-drone" ? { ...ship, position: [0, 0, 0] } : { ...ship, position: [900, 0, 900] }), projectiles: [{ id: "e2e-drone-shot", owner: "player", kind: "laser", position: [0, 0, 0], direction: [0, 0, 0], speed: 0, damage: 999, life: 1, targetId: "scout-drone" }] } }); (e2e.getState() as { tick: (delta: number) => void }).tick(0.05); }); // The kill must be observable through the player-facing surface, not only in the store. await expect(page.getByTestId("story-notification")).toContainText("Boss Defeated"); await expect(page.getByTestId("story-tracker")).toContainText("Drone Prime"); // ... second boss by the same recipe, then salvage recovery and the debrief ... }); Three properties of the runtime, not of the test, are what make this test writable in 140 lines and runnable in commit-triggered pipeline. First, the games state store is exposed to the test process as window.__SPACERPG_E2E__, so the test both reads state (getState()) and writes it (setState()) in the same address space the game runs in. Second, the simulation step is itself callable: tick(0.05) advances physics and combat by one fixed 50 ms increment, which converts destroy boss from real-time skill problem into deterministic state edit (place the target at the origin, exile the other enemies to [900, 0, 900] so they cannot interfere, inject projectile with damage: 999, and step once). Third, the rendered result stays queryable: because the view is DOM, the test can insist that the kill be visible on the player-facing surface (story-notification, story-tracker) rather than only in the store, which is what keeps the shortcut shortcut in how the state is reached and not weakening of the oracle. Outside the boss-kill shortcut, which edits positions directly, the writes are not arbitrary state injection: closeDialogue and the elided travel, docking, and mission-completion steps call the same store actions the UI dispatches, so the state the assertions see is production state player could also have reached. The cheap end, at scale. SpaceRPG demonstrates the strongest case, but test counts alone do not establish GUI coverage. Table 4 therefore separates repository scale and static complexity from test depth and runtime affordances. The five browser projects are larger (50.6299.7 kLOC versus 2.857.6 kLOC), while both groups have P90 cyclomatic complexity between 4 and 8 and overlapping densities of high-complexity functions. All five browser projects run behavioral tests in CI; none of the nine engine projects does. The browser projects 10,850 tests are nevertheless primarily unit, reducer, headless-simulation, jsdom, and API-integration tests rather than GUI E2E tests. Only OpenFrontIO includes real-browser, interaction-reaching harness, and that harness sits outside its default CI suite, so no commit-triggered run exercises it. OpenFrontIOs real-browser harness is not in default CI. The reported browser test counts are predominantly non-GUI tests. We measured coverage rather than trusting repository badges: each browser repositorys own test command was run at its default branch under coverage tool (vitest with the V8 provider for PokéRogue and OpenFront, jest for Hanabi Live, c8 over mocha for Pokémon Showdown, and nyc over mocha for Habitica), with line coverage taken over the repositorys own source. Pokémon Showdowns 38.4% includes large static data tables; its battle simulator alone reaches 83.5%. Habiticas full suite requires MongoDB, so we ran its three independent suites covering shared game rules; the other repositories ran every loadable suite. The supplementary evidence records the scripts, scopes, commits, and raw counts behind every metric and classification in Table 4. The expensive end: engine-backed software. The three properties are not available as uniform automationready surface in self-rendered engine. shipped Unity, Godot, or Unreal build presents an external harness with native process and pixels; its internal state, scene/UI tree, and clock are not exposed as stable outof-process read/write, query, and step APIs. Some surveyed games persist saves, provide local console, or carry narrow multiplayer protocol (P in Table 4), but adapting any of these requires application-specific instrumentation. The consequence is visible across vendors: all three engines ship test framework, yet these projects leave it unused. We surveyed 47 open-source playable games on GitHub (22 on Unity, 14 on Godot, and 11 on Unreal), excluding engines, libraries, editor tooling, and asset collections. Table 4 reports three per engine, chosen to span genres, popularity, and maintenance activity and to include the two used by DeepStateBench. Across these nine projects, none declares Unity [Test] or [UnityTest] method, Godot GUT or gdUnit4 suite, or an Unreal IMPLEMENT_*_AUTOMATION_TEST, BEGIN_DEFINE_SPEC, or FAutomationTestBase declaration. We verified each zero from local clone and confirmed that each clone contains the games source, ruling out both GitHub code-search limitations and missing source files in partial checkout. Across the wider survey the picture is the same on all three engines. Seventeen of the 22 Unity projects contain no first-party automated test. Twelve of the 14 Godot projects install no test framework; the two exceptions are Thrive (3,699 stars), which maintains real gdUnit4 suite, and OpenVic (471), which ships the gdUnit4 addon over directory holding only placeholder file. None of the 11 Unreal projects declares an automation test in first-party source; the single Tests/ directory the survey turned up, in WarriOrb (340), belongs to vendored third-party dialogue plugin. Directories named Test/ or tests/ rarely hold tests (Relintai/broken_seals game/tests/ contains debug scenes, and jynews two using NUnit.Framework lines are unused editor-inserted imports), and four of the nine projects run 19 GitHub Actions workflows on their default branch, none of which executes test. The projects that do carry tests make the pattern precise: engine developers test only what is reachable without the engine. Unity-Technologies/FPSSample (5,129 stars), for example, places every test in an Editor-only assembly over network serialization and delta compression, and Thrives gdUnit4 suite follows the same rule. Across all 47 projects the survey contains exactly one test that renders at all, in Unity-Technologies/BoatAttack (2,781): single [UnityTest] that loads scene and compares one camera frame against reference image. Even that one asserts scenes initial render rather than any state reached by playing, so not single test in the survey drives game to state that requires interaction to reach. The contrast isolates what this paper pays for. Writing the SpaceRPG test required no infrastructure work: the browser had already granted the harness state handle, steppable clock, and queryable view. Obtaining the equivalent for an engine-backed title requires building each of those affordances first, per-application cost that no individual test amortizes, which is why it does not get paid, and why 1,694 merged pull requests across nine games on three engines ship with no automated coverage. StatePortal therefore separates the two costs and automates both: an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes the hook and its capability contract once per application (440 and 456 added lines for PAL3 and jynew, driver and self-tests included, with no product logic rewritten; Table 11), after which checkpoint for new target state is synthesized once per test.

B.5 Task-Provenance Pipeline Details This section expands the three-stage pipeline of Section 4.2 and its phrasing step, giving the signals, weights, execution steps, and guard variants behind each stage and the gates of Table 8. Selection signals and weights. Three per-function signals are computed with single off-the-shelf analyzer, lizard (covering JS/TS/C#/C++/Python/Lua under one definition): McCabe cyclomatic complexity, nesting depth, NLOC, and token count [30]; name-based, non-call-graph textual fan-in/fan-out proxy in the spirit of HenryKafura information-flow coupling [16]; and git churn (commits plus 0.01 changed lines) following the classical churndefect-density signal [34]. Each signal is converted to within-corpus percentile rank before being combined, so that signal with much larger raw scale cannot dominate the composite; the composite score weights complexity 0.35, nesting 0.20, fan-in 0.10, fan-out 0.10, and churn 0.25, with trivial getters/setters and anonymous functions (complexity < 3) removed before ranking. These weights were frozen before any ranking was produced, under versioned, content-hashed configuration (v1.0-preregistered-2026-07) that every downstream artifact records, so report can cite the configuration that produced its ranking. Intersection granularity follows each profiles controllable-surface shape: 2048 requires candidates to land on concrete symbol anchor, while Luantis controllable surface is the entire registry driven by test worldmod (which can write any registered node/meta/player state), so no anchor filter applies there. The top-ranked region for 2048 is GameManager.prototype.move (final score 0.812; cyclomatic complexity 4, nesting 3, fan-out 15, 122 commits), matching the region all eight 2048 tasks 22 target; for Luanti, the top three among 1,587 Lua functions are core.item_place_node, core.node_dig, and falling.lua::set_node, the core routines that mutate world state. From-scratch unreachability diagnostic. This is 2048-specific, bounded-playout diagnostic that quantifies why given target cannot be reached by playing from scratch within budget; it is not cross-benchmark selection signal. Monte-Carlo playout under 2048s own rules [31] (a greedy immediate-merge policy, 200 trials, several-thousand-step budget) reaches given tile value from scratch with sharply declining probability: about 0.99 for 64, 0.88 for 128, 0.43 for 256, and near 0 for 512 and above. Because greedy policy is stronger than random one, this estimate is conservative; we do not claim these tile values are unreachable in principle, only that stronger 2048 heuristic could reach them. What carries weight is narrower: the near-win task fixes one specific, score-consistent board (two tiles of 1024 awaiting winning merge) that almost never appears as the exact post-state of an ordinary from-scratch playout within budget, so that behavior is only exercisable on constructed checkpoint. This signal enters the final task score multiplicatively rather than being averaged in (final = composite (0.5 + 0.5 unreach)), because its natural grain is candidate target, not function. Luanti has neither cheap faithful simulator nor from-scratch generator for arbitrary constructed deep structure, so it is assigned the documented conservative default of 1.0 rather than an estimated number. Ground-truth recording. The selected regions control-flow branches mechanically induce branch-covering seed states, one per task: 2048s three move branches yield its three pilot tasks (a merge branch, win branch, and terminated/no-moves branch). Each scenario runs five fixed steps: pin Math.random to fixed value so the post-move new-tile placement is deterministic and the recorded ground truth is itself replayable; restore the seed board through the games own persistence path (localStorage); call the games real move through the __WARPTEST_2048__ test-gated hook; read back getState(), whose after-state is the ground truth; and record the assertion as the replay-stable projection of that state (score delta, resulting tile value, terminal flag, plus no_severe_console). The only human input is the seed board and the bounded follow-on action, both derived from the regions branches; the post-state is computed by the game itself. Restricting assertions to the replay-stable projection is what lets the same assertion hold on an unpinned, ordinary run (Gate B). Luantis ground truth reuses the same worldmod path; where the engine cannot host given scenario, synthesis reports neutral blocked rather than failure. Mutation operators and kill-rate accounting. Mutants are confined to the selected regions line span (the move-handling region in 2048), so mutant only perturbs code the task claims to cover. Operators are language-agnostic, single-point textual mutations [9, 18]: relational-operator swaps, arithmetic-operator swaps, boolean flips, and small constant perturbations (e.g., 2048 4096), at most three per operator. Mutants that error out for syntactic or environmental reasons are removed from the denominator rather than counted as survivors. The registered protocol c1_start_gate_protocol fixes the sequence semantic_start_grade, before_visual_grade_under_runtime_hold, phase_b_only_if_start_passed, after_semantic_and_visual_grade, and every run index must agree with the manifest copy. Concretely, the harness captures the start frame at the Phase boundary, then reads and grades the programmatic state while the runtime still runs freely; programmatic failure short-circuits without acquiring hold or issuing any visual request. Only after the programmatic start grade passes does the harness suspend the runtime, send the single beforejudge request, release the runtime, and enter Phase B. The after-state grades then run unheld, because no further execution depends on their outcome. What the hold covers. The hold brackets the visual verdict and the transition into Phase B, not the capture and not the programmatic read. It guarantees that the frame shown to the judge is still the live state when the verdict returns, and that Phase departs from exactly the state both oracles accepted; it does not make the two reads simultaneous. Simultaneity is unavailable on the native profiles, where SIGSTOP freezes the same process that serves the programmatic read, so that read must precede the hold. The residual exposure is the interval between capture and hold acquisition, which contains local state read and no model request. Per-profile backends. Browser-hosted profiles (2048, SpaceRPG, DatingSim) and JupyterLab are held through Chromium DevTools session with Emulation.setScriptExecutionDisabled, recorded as backend chromium_cdp_script_pause. Luanti, the two Unity benchmarks (PAL3 and jynew), OpenRA, Blender, and LibreOffice are held at the operating-system process boundary with SIGSTOP and resumed with SIGCONT, recorded 29 as sigstop; the Unity and OpenRA sessions expose the pid of the live application process for this purpose. There is no engine-level time-scale freeze for Unity: every native profile is suspended at the process boundary. Which arms are held. The Start-grading protocol specifies runtime hold for Agent S3, Agent S3 w/ Checkpoint, StatePortal, and the delegated diagnostic, with the applicable configurations listed in arms_under_runtime_hold. On the state-managed Unity path, the adapter closes before visual grading, so the captured Start is evaluated after the runtime has terminated. This case records backend runtime_terminated_before_grading with required and held both false; the protocol permits that backend only for this configuration and benchmark pair. Failure handling and audit record. hold is attempted once, with no retry and no settling delay. If it cannot be acquired the visual judge is never called; if it cannot be released the error is raised rather than swallowed. Either way the trial is recorded as an incomplete infrastructure failure rather than scored outcome, so hold defect can neither inflate nor deflate success rates. Every trial that started visual grading carries start_grading_runtime_hold with required, held, released, backend, and, on native profiles, held_pid. Aggregation rejects report whose recorded backend differs from the one expected for that benchmark, whose hold was not both taken and released, whose native held_pid differs from the process id in the same trials seed evidence, or which claims hold without having run the visual start grade. B.20 Fail-to-Pass and Pass-to-Pass Tests Definitions. Benchmarks built from real repairs label repositorys registered tests by how their verdicts change across the landed fix [19]. fail-to-pass (F2P) test fails on the pre-fix tree and passes on the post-fix it is the executable statement of what the repair was supposed to change, and candidate patch is tree: graded correct when it turns every F2P test green. pass-to-pass (P2P) test passes on both trees: it states what the repair must leave alone, and it is the regression guard that stops patch from buying its F2P verdict by breaking something else. Both labels are properties of test relative to specific pair of trees rather than of the tests source, and both are established by executing the suite on each tree rather than by reading the patch. Why P2P-only population is the treatment target. Patch benchmarks begin from at least one F2P test and ask method to produce the patch that makes it pass. The latent-defect study does not ask for patch the repair has already landed and both trees are real and instead studies the complementary blind spot: repairs for which no F2P test exists upstream, so that the failure signal patch grader would read simply is not there. Recovering that signal from the issue text is itself unreliable, succeeding on roughly one third of real issues or fewer [3, 32], and it is least available exactly where interactive software fails, in defects confined to the rendered result [29]. Such defect is visible in the real rendered or interactive output analogous to game object visibly crossing wall while the software and its existing tests continue to run. F2P absence is therefore an admission requirement of this population, not gap in our evidence: it is what makes an admitted repair case the registered suite cannot decide. 37 The two roles P2P plays here. As an admission criterion, non-empty P2P set that is green on the fixed and on the reversed tree makes the absence of failure signal measured property of the registered suite rather than an untested assumption: the tests run, and they do not notice the defect. As per-trial control, the same set is executed on the clone the trial actually drives, so that rendered difference is attributable to the defect rather than to broken build; the buggy tree is obtained by reversing real production hunks, and reversal that disturbed unrelated behavior would surface as P2P failure. P2P failure consequently blocks the trial instead of counting as defect evidence, and any test discovered to be F2P disqualifies the task. B.22 Fuzzing Study: Mechanism and Campaign Mechanism. validated deep state is also cheap seed for exploring the states around it, which from-scratch replay or scripted GUI testing rarely reaches. Seeded with validated checkpoint, an LLM-driven evolutionary loop proposes neighborhood states with one of four mutation operators (field substitution, unexpected-key insertion, subtree regeneration, and type flip), chosen by Thompson-sampling bandit over each operators yield. Each mutated state is injected through the same warm-session restore path as an ordinary checkpoint, and robustness oracle labels the result defect (the software misbehaves on well-formed state), robust (it handles the mutation gracefully), or rejected (it correctly refuses an invalid state). Only defect outcomes are counted, so an operator cannot inflate its yield by proposing states that are merely invalid. Defects are deduplicated by deterministic fingerprint over the failure signature, and each carries its mutated state as model-free reproduction. The search is economical only because restoring one more state inside warm session is cheap (Section 5.1.2); otherwise every candidate would cost full restart. Campaign on SpaceRPG. We ran the fuzzing study as one unattended campaign against the SpaceRPG profile, seeded from its checkpoints validated in the performance study; it surfaced the 67 deduplicated defects in Table 26. Mutations entered through five injection modes: three write the games own persisted save keys, and two write the live store through the DEV-gated __SPACERPG_E2E__ hook that production builds compile out. Reachability is therefore mechanical label rather than judgment call. The 55 player-reachable defects arrive through the production save loader, exactly as hand-edited save or one written before schema change would; the 12 hook-only defects are resilience gaps rather than player-facing bugs. The dominant player-reachable class is one programmatic oracle would miss: the crafted save loads without error and every state assertion holds, so the failure appears only in the rendered frame, the separation Section 4.3 is built around.
